decisions.quote: The results of the present study replicated those reported by Rogers and Feller (2016): Peer excellence can discourage (rather than elevate) student motivation.
decisions.reason: In the abstract, confirming the discouragement-by-exposure-to-peer-excellence effect is scoped to the traditional-student subgroup and contrasted with its absence among nontraditional college students (a novel population moderator extending Rogers and Feller's 2016 Study 2 MTurk sample). In the publisher conclusions preview, however, the author states an explicit whole-study verdict: 'The results of the present study replicated those reported by Rogers and Feller (2016): Peer excellence can discourage (rather than elevate) student motivation.' Rather than merely asserting a focal subgroup effect, this conclusion takes 'The results of the present study' as a whole as its subject, names Rogers and Feller (2016) directly, and frames the original claim as the proposition that peer excellence 'can' discourage student motivation, which holds despite the nontraditional-student boundary condition. Judging strictly from the supplied abstract and previews without assuming any unseen continuation, this statement constitutes an overall replication verdict under Codebook Rule 1 that outweighs the subgroup contrast and yields 'successful'.

scope_review.parent_objection: The supplied source includes a publisher Conclusions preview stating: The results of the present study replicated those reported by Rogers and Feller (2016): Peer excellence can discourage (rather than elevate) student motivation. First reply discounts this as single-sentence preview and codes mixed across student subgroups. Under codebook Rule1 a genuine overall verdict wins even against individual contrasts, but focal-effect confirmation does not. Is this Conclusions statement a genuine overall post-contrast replication verdict on the study, or merely assertion of a focal effect in traditional students? Only abstract and previews are available; do not assume unseen continuation. Explain whole-study versus focal scope and available evidence limits; return exact codebook outcome, or undeterminable if insufficient.

prior_reply.quote: The results showed that traditional college students were less likely to write another essay if they had previously evaluated exemplary essays relative to poorly-written essays, replicating the discouragement-by-exposure-to-peer-excellence effect. However, the effect was absent among nontraditional college students.
prior_reply.reason: The study set out to test the discouragement-by-peer-excellence effect from Rogers and Feller (2016) across both traditional and nontraditional college students, finding that the effect replicated in traditional students but was absent in nontraditional students. Because the complete abstract explicitly frames the evidence as holding in one target subgroup and failing in the other, the outcome is mixed rather than purely successful based on the single-sentence conclusion preview.
